prog-disc-heading: Specialise in Two of Six Indigenous Disciplines
prog-intro:
Before any student touches clay, metal, leather, bamboo or wood at DIAT, they spend
        dedicated time in Product Design, the foundational strand that runs across
        all year groups from first year through to final year. This is not a separate discipline
        but the intellectual and technical spine of the entire DIAT curriculum.
prog-pd-desc:
Product Design at DIAT equips every student with Computer-Aided Design (CAD)
          software skills and systematic design methodology before they begin production
          in any craft discipline. Students learn to conceptualise, visualise, and
          technically specify their intended artworks digitally, producing detailed
          CAD drawings and 3D models of pieces before commencing physical production.
prog-pd-desc2:
This CAD-to-craft approach bridges indigenous tradition with contemporary
          design technology, producing graduates who can communicate their work
          professionally to clients, galleries, and global markets, a capability
          that directly underpins DIAT's commercial art services arm and the
          international competitiveness of its graduates.
disc-product-intro1:
Product Design is not one discipline among six at DIAT — it is the
        intellectual and technical spine that holds all six together. Every student,
        regardless of their chosen craft specialisation, studies Product Design from
       first year through to final year. Before any student throws clay, cuts leather,
        welds metal, carves wood or lattes bamboo, they have already designed what they     intend to make digitally, precisely, and professionally.
disc-product-intro2:
At DIAT, Product Design means learning to use Computer-Aided Design (CAD)
        software to produce technical drawings, 3D models, and rendered visualisations
        of craft objects before physical production begins. Students learn to write design
        briefs, specify materials, calculate dimensions, and present their concepts to
        a professional standard, the skills that allow a DIAT graduate to walk
        into any client meeting, gallery, or design competition and communicate their
        work with authority.
comm-hero-sub: DIAT's academic work does not end in the studio. Through a structured three-month internship programme, students are embedded with artisan communities across Ghana learning, documenting and formally attributing the indigenous craft knowledge that sustains the department.

about-hero-sub:
From a Diploma programme founded in 1976 to Ghana's premier academic institution
      for indigenous art and craft education, the story of DIAT is the story of
      a nation's heritage reclaimed, formalised, and carried forward.
about-para-1:
Founded in 1976 as a Diploma programme, the then Department of Integrated Rural Art and
          Industry (IRAI), now the Department of Indigenous Art and Technology (DIAT) at the
          Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) is Ghana's pioneering
          institution for indigenous art education, uniquely combining Academia, commercial craft
          production, and active Community engagement under one roof.
about-para-2:
Operating under the College of Art and Built Environment - CABE at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology - KNUST, DIAT has for five decades served as the foremost academic custodian of Ghana's indigenous craft traditions from  Clay and Earthenware, Fibres and Fabrics, Leather Design and Technology, Metal Production and Fabrication, Rattan and Bamboo Processing, and Wood and Furniture. The department's mandate is not merely to preserve these traditions but to innovate within them, equipping each generation of practitioners with both the cultural knowledge and the contemporary design tools needed to carry indigenous craft into the global marketplace.
Through project-based learning, students in each of the six (6) disciplines receive the necessary entrepreneurial training and skills to create artworks that incorporate with at least one of DIAT's philosophies: indigenous concepts, integration concepts, material integration, or technology integration of one or more of the six (6) disciplines. The department then preserves and markets these artworks for public consumption.
about-para-3: Our structured curriculum is centered around six core disciplines with Product Design as the base. Clay and Earthenware, Fibres and Fabrics, Leather Design and Technology, Metal Production and Fabrication, Rattan and Bamboo Processing, and Wood and Furniture programmes ground every student in Product Design from first year, equipping them with Computer-Aided Design (CAD) tools and design methodology before guiding them into mastery of two of six indigenous craft disciplines. This CAD-to-craft approach designing digitally before making by hand is a major part of what makes DIAT graduates uniquely competitive: they are simultaneously cultural custodians and contemporary design professionals.
about-ann-body:
DIAT marks half a century of preserving, formalising, and promoting
          Ghana’s indigenous craft heritage within one of Africa’s foremost technical universities.
about-hist-body:
The story of the Department of Indigenous Art and Technology (DIAT) at Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) is one of vision, resilience, and transformation. Founded in 1976 as the Integrated Rural Art and Industry program, its original mission was clear: to harness Ghana’s rich indigenous art traditions and channel them into sustainable rural industries. At a time when modernisation threatened to overshadow traditional crafts, the department served as a guardian of heritage, ensuring that weaving, carving, dyeing, and other indigenous practices were not only preserved but also reimagined for contemporary relevance.
In its early years, the department offered a diploma program that focused on practical skills for rural artisans and students. The emphasis was on cottage industries (small-scale enterprises) that could empower communities economically while safeguarding cultural identity. Students were trained to become both artisans and entrepreneurs, capable of producing crafts that embodied Ghanaian tradition while meeting the demands of modern markets.
By the 1990s, the department recognised that indigenous art could not remain static. It began to integrate technology and design innovation, preparing students to navigate a rapidly globalising creative economy. This evolution culminated in 1999 when the diploma program was upgraded to a degree program, marking a significant academic milestone. The transition reflected not only the department’s growing reputation but also its alignment with national development goals by producing graduates who could lead in both cultural preservation and industrial innovation.
The new millennium brought further transformation. The department rebranded as the Department of Indigenous Art and Technology (DIAT), a name that captured its dual commitment: safeguarding indigenous knowledge while embracing technological advancement. Graduate programs—MPhil and PhD—were introduced, positioning DIAT as a hub for advanced research in indigenous art-tech innovation, sustainable textiles, and cultural entrepreneurship. This academic expansion allowed DIAT to contribute to global discussions on sustainability, heritage, and creative industries while remaining deeply rooted in Ghanaian traditions.
Beyond academia, DIAT has had a profound impact on community empowerment. Through apprenticeship models, cooperative organisations, and rural outreach, the department has linked artisans to modern markets, fostered fair-trade practices, and nurtured community resilience. Its graduates have established creative enterprises, revitalised endangered crafts, and championed cultural education. In doing so, DIAT has become more than just an academic department; it is a movement that bridges tradition and modernity, rural and urban, local and global.
Today, DIAT embodies cultural resilience by preserving Ghana’s artistic heritage against the forces of globalisation. It demonstrates academic innovation by integrating indigenous knowledge with modern design, sustainability, and digital technology. Moreover, it advances community empowerment by equipping artisans and graduates to transform their communities through creativity and entrepreneurship.
This journey from a rural art diploma in 1976 to a globally relevant academic department justifies the celebration of DIAT. Its wealth is not measured in material terms alone but in cultural capital, academic excellence, and social impact. DIAT stands as a testament to Ghana’s ability to honour its past while shaping its future, making its celebration both necessary and inspiring.
